blocks.text: Materials have specific uses depending on their characteristics and properties, such as hardness, ductility and malleability. What makes steel hard and lead soft? It depends on the structure, the particular order and bonding of atoms and molecules in a material. Similarly, the study of fluids in motion is relatively complicated, but the analysis can be simplified by making a few assumptions and by using two conservation principles, the conservation of mass and the conservation of energy: the law of conservation of mass gives the equation of continuity, while the law of conservation of energy is the basis of Bernoulli's theorem.

In crystalline solids there is a regular arrangement of atoms and molecules: the neighbours of every molecule are arranged in a regular pattern that is consistent throughout the crystal, so there is an ordered structure. Most solids, like metals and ceramics, have a crystalline structure. The arrangement of molecules, atoms or ions within all types of crystalline solids can be studied by techniques such as X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Atoms, molecules or ions in a crystalline solid are not static: each atom vibrates about a fixed point with an amplitude that increases with temperature; it is the average atomic positions that are perfectly ordered over large distances. The cohesive forces between atoms, molecules or ions maintain the strict long-range order in spite of the vibrations. For every crystal, however, there is a temperature at which the vibrations become so great that the structure suddenly breaks up and the solid melts; the transition from solid (order) to liquid (disorder) is therefore abrupt or discontinuous, and every crystalline solid has a definite melting point, for example quartz, calcite, sugar, mica and diamond.

blocks.text: The word amorphous means without form or structure: in amorphous solids there is no regular arrangement of molecules like that in crystalline solids, so amorphous solids are more like liquids with the disordered structure frozen in. Ordinary glass, a solid at ordinary temperature, has no regular arrangement of molecules; on heating it gradually softens into a paste-like state before it becomes a very viscous liquid at almost 800 degrees C. Amorphous solids are also called glassy solids; they have no definite melting point, for example plastic, glass and fused silicon.

blocks.alt: Left, labelled Crystalline solids: identical teal balls packed in straight rows and columns, with a second layer showing in the gaps. Right, labelled Amorphous solids: the same balls scattered with no regular arrangement and uneven gaps between them.
blocks.caption: Crystalline solids and amorphous solids (PDF page 94) (original drawing after the textbook's picture).

blocks.text: Polymers are solid materials with a structure intermediate between order and disorder; they can be classified as partially or poorly crystalline solids. Polymers form a large group of naturally occurring and synthetic materials. Plastics and synthetic rubbers are termed polymers because they are formed by polymerization reactions in which relatively simple molecules are chemically combined into massive long-chain molecules or three-dimensional structures. These materials have rather low specific gravity compared with even the lightest metals, yet exhibit a good strength-to-weight ratio. Polymers consist wholly or in part of a chemical combination of carbon with oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen and other metallic or non-metallic elements; polythene, polystyrene and nylon are examples, and natural rubber in the pure state is entirely a hydrocarbon of formula (C5H8)n. The side box shows part of a PVC molecule, a chain of carbon atoms carrying hydrogen and chlorine.
